lines.text: My grandfather wrote a letter to his sister in Ipoh every month for sixty years.
He never trusted the telephone, because he owned one for most of that time.
lines.note: Connector: owning a telephone and not trusting it is a contrast, so it is 'although'.

lines.text: Each letter took him an entire evening. He would sit by the window
on a fountain pen and a dictionary, choosing every word with great care.
lines.note: Preposition: he sits 'with' the things he uses.

lines.text: As a child, I find this habit strange, since a message could be
lines.note: Tense: 'as a child' is in the past, so it is 'found'.

lines.text: sent in seconds. It was only after his dead that I understood. Among
lines.note: Word form: after 'his' a noun is needed — 'death'.

lines.text: his belongings was a biscuit tin holding every reply his sister had ever wrote.
lines.note: Verb form: after 'had ever' it is 'written'.

lines.text: The letters were arranged by year and tied with string. Reading them, I
discovered a brother and sister who has shared every joy and every worry
lines.note: Tense: the story is in the past, so it is 'had shared'.

lines.text: across four hundred kilometres. A telephone call ends, and a letter can be
lines.note: Connector: a call that ends and a letter that lasts are a contrast, so it is 'but'.

lines.text: read again and again. I have since begun write to my own cousin,
and the first reply arrived last week in a biscuit-coloured envelope.
